entry.title: The Witcher 4 Is Made with Console-First Approach; 60 FPS on Xbox Series S Will Be 'Extremely Challenging' to Achieve, Says CDPR
entry.summary:
The Witcher 4 Goes Console-First
CDPR’s VP of Technology, Charles Tremblay, revealed in a recent Digital Foundry sit-down that The Witcher 4 is being built around a console-first Unreal Engine pipeline. The ambitious goal? A fully ray-traced open world running at 60 FPS on PS5—with everything else stripped back for now to nail performance rather than scaling down from a beefy PC build. Challenges Ahead
While the tech demo looks gorgeous, it’s not a full gameplay loop yet, and getting 60 FPS on Xbox Series S “will be extremely challenging,” Tremblay admits. They’ve already swapped to hardware Lumen RT and plan to scale up for high-end PCs, but plenty of optimization lies ahead. The Witcher 4 is tentatively slated for 2027 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S|X.

entry.title: XREAL Project Aura: AR Glasses with up to 70 FoV - New X1S chip in the glasses and a Snapdragon in the puck
entry.summary: TL;DR: Xreal’s Project Aura is shaping up to be the first true AR glasses running Google’s Android XR—but your phone can’t power them. Instead of offloading all that 3D and AI muscle to a tethered phone, Aura uses a pocketable “compute puck” (likely packing a Snapdragon XR chip) while the glasses themselves house a more powerful X1S processor. Expect front-facing sensors and hand-tracking, but also a wired connection and uncertain battery life for heavy use. On the optics side, Aura ditches the bulky “birdbath” lenses for a new flat-prism design that’s about 44 percent smaller yet pushes your field of view up to ~70 degrees. It’ll run most Android apps (think Google Maps with 3D overlays) and play nice with Gemini AI demos, but with no word on price or release date—rumor has it these could cost near $1,000—so don’t bet on walking around wire-free anytime soon.

entry.title: IBM aims to build the world's first large-scale, error-corrected quantum computer by 2028
entry.summary:
IBM’s Quantum Leap
IBM just unveiled its roadmap to build Starling, a modular, error-corrected quantum computer by 2028 (cloud-ready in 2029). Housed in a new Poughkeepsie data center, Starling will network dozens of chip modules to deliver 200 logical qubits—enough to run some 100 million fault-tolerant operations in a row, compared with today’s few thousand. Cracking the Error-Correction Code
The secret sauce is IBM’s low-density parity-check error-correction scheme (about 12 physical qubits per logical qubit), paired with real-time decoding on FPGAs. After smaller demos—Loon (2025), Kookaburra (2026), Cockatoo (2027)—IBM will scale up to ~100 modules for Starling, then dream even bigger with “Blue Jay” (2,000 logical qubits) down the road. Challenges remain, but IBM says it’s moved from science to engineering in the quantum race.
